how: The words “Everyone knows” make the claim sound like common knowledge, and rest the claim on how widely it is held, not on reasons. The sentence does not say what evidence the agreement rests on or who exactly agrees.

The words “it is widely accepted” offer broad agreement as the reason to accept the claim, and lean on agreement without showing what it rests on. The sentence does not say what evidence the agreement rests on or how the agreement was measured.

The words “Studies show” cite studies or experts without saying which ones, and lend the claim the weight of research or authority. The sentence does not say which studies it means or where a reader could find the source.

The words “Data shows” name a kind of support instead of a source to check, and lend the claim the weight of research or authority. The sentence does not say where the data comes from, what exactly was found or how the result was measured.

The word “misinformation” labels those who disagree instead of answering them, and sets the opposing view aside without addressing what it says. The sentence does not say what evidence the label rests on or what those holding the view base it on.

The words “has been thoroughly debunked” give a verdict without showing how it was reached, and set the opposing view aside without addressing what it says. The sentence does not say what evidence the label rests on or where a reader could check the verdict.

The words “the inevitable direction” present the outcome as already decided, and treat where things are heading as the reason to agree. The sentence does not say what the forecast rests on, which past events are meant or what the case for the outcome is.

The words “there is no stopping this” suggest there is no point in pushing back, and offer a sense of momentum in place of a reason. The sentence does not say what the forecast rests on, what the case for the outcome is or which past events are meant.

The words “we've always done it this way” offer a practice's age as the reason to keep it, and point to a practice's history, not its results. The sentence does not say what results the practice has produced or whether the practice's original reasons still apply.

The words “departing from tradition would be unwise” treat a long-held custom as needing no defense, and let precedent stand in for an argument about this case. The sentence does not say what would happen if the practice changed or what results the practice has produced.

The words “both sides make good points” set the views side by side as equally supported, and skip the step of comparing the evidence behind each view. The sentence does not say how the evidence for each view compares or why the views get equal weight.

The words “the truth lies somewhere in the middle” make an even split sound like the careful position, and skip the step of comparing the evidence behind each view. The sentence does not say how the evidence for each view compares or what the middle position would be.

The words “The vast majority of our garden club members agree” cite a majority without showing it, and give the claim the weight of agreement without showing the agreement. The sentence does not say how the support was measured, who was asked or what findings the agreement is based on.

The words “growing consensus suggests” suggest agreement is growing without saying whose, and claim wide support without saying where it comes from. The sentence does not say who agrees, what findings the agreement is based on or over what period the support has grown.

The words “Our goal is to” offer an intention where a result might be expected, and state a goal without saying how far it has been reached. The sentence does not say what has been achieved so far or how progress toward the goal is measured.

The words “we strive to deliver” offer an intention where a result might be expected, and put a promise where a number or a date could go. The sentence does not say what result a reader could check or what has been achieved so far.

The words “the misguided schedule” fold a judgment into what reads as a plain description, and name the subject in a way that already judges it. The sentence does not say who holds this view or what the label is based on.

The words “The so-called upgrade” name the subject in a way that already judges it, and fold a judgment into what reads as a plain description. The sentence does not say what the label is based on or who holds this view.

The word “"improved"” casts doubt through quotation marks without saying why, and signals doubt without offering a fact to weigh. The sentence does not say why the term is in quotation marks, what fact would show whether the term fits or who is being quoted.
The word “"homemade"” leaves the reader to guess what the quotation marks mean, and carries a hint of doubt that is never stated. The sentence does not say what the quotation marks signal here.

The word “claimed” adds doubt or attitude where a plain verb would do, and reports speech with a verb that carries a judgment. The sentence does not say what the choice of verb is based on or what evidence the speaker offered.

The word “alleged” adds doubt or attitude where a plain verb would do, and reports speech with a verb that carries a judgment. The sentence does not say what the choice of verb is based on or what evidence the speaker offered.

The words “top firms all use” describe only the winners, not the whole group, and make a shared trait look like the reason for success. The sentence does not say whether the ones that failed did the same thing, how many tried and failed or what else might explain the result.

The words “Either we raise the bake sale prices this year or” present a pair of options as the only ones, and cast one option as the only way to avoid the other. The sentence does not say what shows these are the only options or whether other options were looked at.

The words “only two options” present a pair of options as the only ones, and narrow the choice to just these options without showing why. The sentence does not say what shows these are the only options or whether other options were looked at.

The words “Act now” shorten the clock on the reader's decision, and press for quick action through alarm or time pressure. The sentence does not say where the deadline comes from or what acting now would change.

The words “Any reasonable person” tie agreeing to being seen as sensible or decent, and put a judgment about the reader where a reason would go. The sentence does not say what evidence the claim rests on or by what standard people are being judged.

The words “How could anyone possibly” cast disagreeing as a lack of sense or care, and make disagreeing or choosing otherwise feel foolish. The sentence does not say why disagreeing or choosing otherwise would be foolish.

The words “simply heartbreaking” put a feeling where a reason would go, and let a strong reaction stand in for the details. The sentence does not say what exactly happened or what facts the feeling responds to.

The words “The devastation speaks for itself” let a strong reaction stand in for the details, and skip past the details straight to the feeling. The sentence does not say what exactly happened or how large the loss is.

The words “Any caring person would agree” frame one view as simply the decent one, and put an appeal to decency where a reason would go. The sentence does not say what reasons the view rests on or what costs and benefits are at stake.

The words “it is simply a matter of basic decency” put an appeal to decency where a reason would go, and frame one view as simply the decent one. The sentence does not say what costs and benefits are at stake or what reasons the view rests on.

The words “simply don't understand the technical requirements” question people's grasp of the subject instead of their point, and make holding the other view sound like a failure to understand. The sentence does not say what the people it describes argue or what reply there is to the point itself.

The words “what they're really asking” present a restatement as what the point really means, and let a restated version stand in for the original point. The sentence does not say what shows the restatement matches what was meant or what answer there is to the original point.

The words “that is really just” treat the point as standing for something beneath its words, and give no evidence that the restatement is what was meant. The sentence does not say what shows the restatement matches what was meant or what answer there is to the original point.

The words “sanctions will be sought” answer the argument with a warning of consequences, and make keeping the argument feel risky. The sentence does not say what grounds the penalty would rest on or what reply the argument gets on its own terms.

The words “seeking sanctions against” make keeping the argument feel risky, and shift attention from the argument to the risk of pressing it. The sentence does not say what reply the argument gets on its own terms or what grounds the penalty would rest on.

The words “Plaintiff claims that every” restate the position in all-or-nothing terms, and make the position, as restated, easy to doubt. The sentence does not say what the original argument said in its own words or whether the position allows any exceptions.

The words “is essentially arguing that we should” put a paraphrase in place of the position's own words, and restate the position in all-or-nothing terms. The sentence does not say what the original argument said in its own words or what the original argument asks for.
The words “Many people” suggest a crowd agrees without saying who or how many, and use a vague amount where a number could go. The sentence does not say who holds the view or how many hold the view.

The words “It is widely believed” make a view sound widely held with no figure given, and suggest a crowd agrees without saying who or how many. The sentence does not say who holds the view or how the size of the group is known.

The word “Shocking” tells the reader how to feel before the details arrive, and opens on a feeling before the facts are given. The sentence does not say what the reaction is based on or who feels this way.

The word “Heartbreaking” tells the reader how to feel before the details arrive, and colors how the rest of the sentence is read. The sentence does not say who feels this way or what the reaction is based on.

The words “is expected to” imply that someone has weighed the odds without naming who, and state a forecast with no forecaster attached. The sentence does not say who expects this outcome or what the expectation is based on.

The words “is poised to” present an outcome as the expected one, and state a forecast with no forecaster attached. The sentence does not say what the expectation is based on or who expects this outcome.

The words “down 45% from the record high” compare the figure with a peak or a low point, and make the figure seem large or small through one comparison. The sentence does not say what the figure is now or what the figure has usually been.

The words “sales will reach $600” speak of a future result as certain, and carry no word such as expected or estimated. The sentence does not say what the claim about the future rests on or what range of outcomes is possible.

The words “the price will fall” speak of a future result as certain, and invite the reader to treat a future result as known. The sentence does not say what the claim about the future rests on or what the outcome depends on.

The words “there's no reason to think this will stop” invite the reader to carry the run forward, and say nothing about why the run would last. The sentence does not say what caused the run or what could change from here.

The words “continues its winning ways” describe a run or trend as still going, and invite the reader to carry the run forward. The sentence does not say what links past results to future ones or what could change from here.

The words “Pursuant to the implementation” wrap a plain point in stiff official language, and use process wording where plain words would say the same. The sentence does not say why the step is being taken or who made the decision.

The words “Notwithstanding the foregoing” wrap a plain point in stiff official language, and use process wording where plain words would say the same. The sentence does not say which earlier point the phrase refers to.

The words “Wellsmere-educated nutritionist says” offer a credential as the reason to believe the claim, and say who is speaking but not what the claim rests on. The sentence does not say what evidence the claim rests on or how the credential bears on this claim.

The words “The transit board has concluded that” report a conclusion without saying what it rests on, and say a finding exists but not how it was reached. The sentence does not say what evidence the conclusion rests on or how the conclusion was reached.

The words “The garden club has found that” report a conclusion without saying what it rests on, and say a finding exists but not how it was reached. The sentence does not say what evidence the conclusion rests on or how the conclusion was reached.

The words “As a neutral third party” claim neutrality or objectivity without showing what backs it, and cast the source as a referee with nothing at stake. The sentence does not say what shows the source has no stake or what evidence the view rests on.

The words “reflects the evidence objectively” claim neutrality or objectivity without showing what backs it, and describe the source's own stance in place of evidence. The sentence does not say what evidence the view rests on or how the evidence was weighed.

The words “Leading organizations recommend” borrow the standing of organizations without naming any, and lean on unnamed authorities to carry the weight of the claim. The sentence does not say who exactly the backers are, what evidence the backing rests on or where the backers' statements can be found.

The words “Industry leaders have long recognized” lean on unnamed authorities to carry the weight of the claim, and use a label of importance in place of a name. The sentence does not say who exactly the backers are or what evidence the backing rests on.

The words “completely destroyed” describe the harm as total and final, and give a verdict on the damage instead of a measure. The sentence does not say how the stated scale was measured or what was checked before the harm was called total.

The words “everything is ruined” describe the harm as total and final, and set no limit on the harm described. The sentence does not say what exactly is said to be damaged or what was checked before the harm was called total.

The words “settled law” present the question as already answered, and close the discussion without showing how the rule fits this case. The sentence does not say how the rule fits the case at hand or how the rule answers the point that was raised.

The words “well settled that” present the question as already answered, and offer a stamp of authority in place of an argument. The sentence does not say which authority it is pointing to or what reasoning stands behind the rule.

The words “plainly meritless” label the argument without answering what it says, and let a strong label do the work of a reason. The sentence does not say what reasoning leads to the label or how the argument's own points are answered.

The words “wholly without merit” label the argument without answering what it says, and let a strong label do the work of a reason. The sentence does not say what reasoning leads to the label or what reasons the argument itself gives.

The words “The weight of authority” give a sense of size without naming any source, and let a pile of authority stand in for reasoning. The sentence does not say which authorities it means or what reasoning those sources gave.

The words “Every court that has addressed” treat the amount of authority as the reason to agree, and sum up many sources in a few words. The sentence does not say which authorities it means or how closely those cases match the present case.

The words “failed to raise” answer with a procedural bar instead of the substance, and draw attention to how, when or by whom the matter was raised. The sentence does not say what answer the point would get on its merits or whether the point can be raised another way.

The words “waived any objection” answer with a procedural bar instead of the substance, and invite the reader to treat the matter as closed. The sentence does not say what answer the point would get on its merits or which rule creates the bar.

The words “People familiar with the discussions” credit the claim to people the reader cannot identify, and suggest inside knowledge without showing what it is. The sentence does not say who the sources are or how the sources know this.

The words “Unnamed sources” credit the claim to people the reader cannot identify, and lend the claim the weight of sources without naming them. The sentence does not say who the sources are or how the sources know this.
